omahaEvents1993: [Jan 1, 1993 | verified] Nebraska Cornhuskers lose the 1993 Orange Bowl to Florida State in the rain (Omaha World-Herald retrospective calls it 'a rainy day for Huskers'; final score 27-14 is from general knowledge, medium confidence). Newspaper headline material for January.

[Apr 16, 1993 | verified] Omaha Royals (Triple-A affiliate of the Kansas City Royals, American Association, playing at Rosenblatt Stadium) home opener; Warren Buffett throws out the first pitch. Billboard idea: 'Royals Baseball at Rosenblatt - Take Me Out to the Ballgame'.

[Spring 1993 | verified] Mayor P.J. Morgan wins re-election; he took 73% in the primary, the largest percentage in city history, against three little-known challengers. (He later resigned in June 1994.) Campaign yard signs / radio news.

[1993 | verified] Casino gambling begins in Missouri in 1993, pulling gamblers away from Ak-Sar-Ben racetrack in Omaha; Ak-Sar-Ben's 1992 average daily attendance of ~3,500 was its lowest in 59 years (vs ~15,000 a decade earlier). A seven-furlong chute was added to the track in 1993. Ak-Sar-Ben is 'Nebraska' spelled backwards. Track closed Aug 7, 1995 (after game period). Billboard idea: 'Live Racing at Ak-Sar-Ben'.

[May 4, 1993 | verified] Omaha Racers (Continental Basketball Association) celebrate their 1992-93 CBA championship with a rally at Westroads Mall; coach Mike Thibault. Home arena was the Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum. Radio chatter / newspaper sports page.

[June 4-12, 1993 | verified] College World Series at Johnny Rosenblatt Stadium. LSU (coach Skip Bertman) beats Wichita State 8-0 in the final on June 12 before 20,286; pitcher Brett Laxton dominates; Most Outstanding Player Todd Walker. LSU's second title. Banners on 13th Street near Rosenblatt / radio play-by-play.
[June 1 - July 27, 1993 | verified] Rain fell at Omaha on 34 of 57 days. Across the Missouri basin it rained somewhere every day from March 14 through July 29. Weather-radio chatter.

[July 1993 | verified] Great Flood of 1993: Missouri River levels from Omaha down to Rulo were the highest since 1952, with record crests at Plattsmouth and Brownville; a peak stage of about 30.2 ft is cited at Omaha (medium confidence on the exact figure). In the Omaha Corps of Engineers district, 9 of 31 federal levees and 173 of 210 non-federal levees failed or were overtopped. 52 Nebraska counties were declared federal disaster areas for flooding and storms in 1993. Headlines: 'River Keeps Rising', sandbag volunteer calls.

[July 22, 1993 | medium] Damaging flash flood in the Papillion Creek watershed (Omaha's west/south-side creek system), per an Army Corps report. Note: the often-quoted '7 killed' Papio figure belongs to the June 1964 flood, NOT 1993. Do not use it for 1993.
[July 27, 1993 | verified] Missouri River crests at a record 48.9 ft at Kansas City, breaking the 1951 record by 2.7 ft. Regional news on the radio.
[July 1993 | general knowledge, medium-high] Des Moines, Iowa loses its city water supply for about 12 days after the flood swamps its water works. National and regional headline.

[June 1, 1992 onward | general knowledge, high] U.S. Strategic Command (STRATCOM) is newly headquartered at Offutt Air Force Base in Bellevue, just south of Omaha, replacing the Strategic Air Command. Background military-jet ambience or base signage.

[1992-1993 | verified] The Lied Jungle at Henry Doorly Zoo (opened April 4, 1992) is billed as the world's largest indoor rainforest. It's a still-new attraction in summer 1993, good for a billboard: 'See the World's Largest Indoor Jungle'.

[1991-1996 | verified] Logan Fontenelle Homes public housing in North Omaha is being demolished after residents won a 1991 civil-rights lawsuit against the Omaha Housing Authority and HUD. It was fully gone by about 1995-96 and replaced by the mixed-income Conestoga neighborhood. In 1993 you could show partially cleared lots and fenced-off buildings.
[Sept 1993 | general knowledge, medium] The Nebraska Lottery launches, with first scratch tickets sold around September 1993. Convenience-store posters.

[Sept-Nov 1993 | verified] Nebraska Cornhuskers (coach Tom Osborne, QB Tommie Frazier; both general knowledge, high) go 11-0 in the regular season and 7-0 in the Big Eight, ranked #2. Saturday radio broadcasts, red 'Go Big Red' flags and bumper stickers everywhere.
[Jan 1, 1994 | verified] Nebraska loses the Orange Bowl 18-16 to #1 Florida State on a missed last-second field goal (useful if the game runs into the new year).

[1993 | general knowledge, high] George Brett's final season with the Kansas City Royals, his last game in early October 1993. On July 2, 1993, Royals Stadium was renamed Kauffman Stadium (medium). KC is the big-league team for many Omaha fans.

[National, 1993 | general knowledge, high] For TV and newspaper filler: Clinton inaugurated (Jan 20); World Trade Center bombing (Feb 26); Waco siege (Feb 28 - Apr 19); federal Rodney King civil-rights verdict (Apr 17); 'Menace II Society' in theaters (May 26); 'Jurassic Park' opens (June 11); Chicago Bulls three-peat (June 20); 'Mortal Monday' home release of Mortal Kombat (Sept 13); Michael Jordan retires (Oct 6); Blue Jays win the World Series on Joe Carter's home run (Oct 23); NAFTA passes Congress (Nov).
[1993 | general knowledge, high] Nebraska officials in 1993: Governor Ben Nelson; U.S. Senators Jim Exon and Bob Kerrey; Omaha-area Rep. Peter Hoagland (medium-high).
weatherAndSeason: Summer 1993 in Omaha was the summer of the Great Flood (verified). It was unusually wet, cloudy and cool. Omaha had measurable rain on 34 of the 57 days from June 1 to July 27, and somewhere in the Missouri basin it rained every day from March 14 to July 29. Midwest climate summaries describe near-constant cloud cover, below-normal temperatures and saturated soils all summer. A stalled boundary between high pressure and storm systems swung back and forth over the central Plains for more than two and a half months. The Missouri River was high, brown and full of debris. In July, river levels from Omaha down to Rulo were the highest since 1952, with record crests just downstream at Plattsmouth and Brownville and a cited peak of about 30.2 ft at Omaha (medium confidence on the exact number). Levees failed widely in the Omaha Corps district (9 of 31 federal, 173 of 210 non-federal), and 52 Nebraska counties became federal disaster areas. Late July brought especially heavy rain to southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, and the Papillion Creek system had a damaging flash flood around July 22 (medium). Suggested game ambience: gray overcast skies, frequent thunderstorms and downpours, puddles and wet asphalt, humid haze, mosquitoes, sandbag walls and 'ROAD CLOSED - HIGH WATER' barricades near the riverfront and low creek crossings, radio weather bulletins and flood-stage updates, and volunteer sandbagging calls. Normal Omaha summers are hot and humid (highs in the upper 80s F). 1993 ran cooler and wetter than usual, so mixing muggy days with rainy ones fits the period. Uncertain: specific Omaha street closures and any 1993 flooding at Eppley Airfield could not be confirmed; my sources on Eppley flooding refer to 2011.
everydayTech1993: Numeric pagers ('beepers') clipped to the belt or waistband: roughly $50-150 to buy plus about $10-20/month for service (general knowledge, approximate). Common numeric codes: 911 = urgent / call now, 411 = what's up / info, 143 = I love you, 07734 = 'hello' read upside down, a phone number followed by a code, and 'call back' repeated digits.

Payphones are everywhere at gas stations, corners and laundromats. A local call is typically 25 cents (some places still 20 cents; approximate). The local phone company was U S WEST (Northwestern Bell folded into U S WEST Communications in 1991; general knowledge, medium-high). Calling cards and collect calls ('1-800-COLLECT' style ads) are common.
Cellular 'brick' and early flip phones exist but are rare and expensive: several hundred to $1,000+ for the handset plus pricey per-minute airtime. Car phones are a status symbol (approximate).
Boomboxes with dual cassette decks, $40-200 (approximate). Car audio culture: pull-out or detachable-faceplate cassette decks, big trunk subwoofers ('bass in the trunk'), amps.

Music formats: cassette albums about $8-10, CDs about $12-16, cassette singles ('cassingles') about $3-4, blank tapes about $1-2 for mixtapes (approximate). Portable players: cassette Walkman $20-60, portable CD 'Discman' about $100-200 (approximate).
VCRs and VHS: rental about $2-3 per night at video stores (approximate).

Video games: Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis, about $99-150 by 1993 (approximate); Game Boy. Home 'Mortal Kombat' released Sept 13, 1993 ('Mortal Monday'). Arcade cabinets in malls and corner stores: Street Fighter II, NBA Jam (1993), Mortal Kombat, at 25-50 cents a play (approximate).
Home phones: corded wall phones, early cordless phones, answering machines with microcassettes; Caller ID boxes just appearing (general knowledge).

Other props: police scanners, CB radios in trucks, disposable and Polaroid cameras, TV antennas and rabbit ears, cable TV with MTV/BET, 'Yo! MTV Raps' and 'Rap City' on TV (general knowledge), newspaper vending boxes, 1-900 hotline ads, fax machines in offices. The public Internet is essentially absent from street life in 1993.
carsCommonIn1993: Boxy late-1970s and 1980s full-size rear-drive sedans: long hoods, square headlights, chrome bumpers, vinyl roofs. The classic 'land yacht' four-door, often older and faded.
Newer rounded 'bubble/whale' full-size sedans (early-1990s redesigns), used as taxis, family cars and unmarked police cars.

Mid-1980s rear-drive two-door 'G-body' style personal coupes with formal rooflines and T-tops. These were street and lowrider favorites: candy paint, gold or chrome wire wheels, skinny whitewall tires with a colored stripe.
1960s full-size convertibles and hardtops set up as lowriders with hydraulics (hopping, three-wheel motion), wire wheels, chain steering wheels and pinstriping.
Wedge-shaped 1980s sports coupes and pony cars (third-generation style), often with louvers, T-tops and mismatched primer panels.
Aerodynamic 'jellybean' mid-size front-drive sedans and wagons (early-1990s style), very common family cars and also the typical shape of Omaha police cruisers at the time (see policeDetails).
Wood-paneled station wagons and first-generation boxy minivans.
Square-body full-size pickups (1973-87 style) and early-1990s pickups, plus lowered 'minitrucks' with graphics and chrome. Pickups are extremely common in Nebraska.
Boxy early SUVs (two- and four-door utes) and full-size conversion vans with small windows, custom stripes and ladders.
Small economy hatchbacks and compacts (often rusty from road salt; Midwest winters mean rust on fender lips and rocker panels).
Luxury 'big body' four-doors and two-doors (formal-roof coupes, long limousine-like sedans), sometimes with gold packages, landau tops and a continental spare-tire kit.

City transit buses (Omaha's system was Metro Area Transit, 'MAT', general knowledge, medium; colors unverified), yellow school buses, livestock and grain trucks near South Omaha and the interstates, and taxis.
policeDetails: Verified: in 1990 the Omaha Police Division (the department's name at the time; now the Omaha Police Department) became the first major U.S. police agency to adopt an intermediate-size front-wheel-drive sedan as its marked cruiser, chosen for cost, fuel economy and maintenance. So a 1993 Omaha patrol car should be a rounded early-90s mid-size front-drive four-door sedan, not the classic boxy full-size rear-drive police sedan. The exact make/model (a Lumina- or Taurus-type car) could not be confirmed. Also verified: OPD painted its cruiser roofs white starting in the 1940s. In 1990 it switched from revolvers to semi-automatic handguns and adopted a restrictive pursuit policy that cut pursuits by about 80%. The new Northeast precinct at 30th & Taylor was not built until 1997, so do not put it in a 1993 map. NOT verified: the exact 1993 paint and livery. Safe generic look for a stylized game: a white or two-tone (dark body, white roof) mid-size sedan, a door emblem or city-style seal with 'POLICE' and a fictionalized city name or 'OMAHA POLICE' lettering, a unit number on the roof/trunk and fenders, a red-and-blue bar light on the roof, a spotlight by the driver's A-pillar, black steel wheels with small hubcaps, and a push bar optional. Many real agencies used exactly this generic scheme in the early 90s. Unmarked cars: plain full-size or mid-size sedans in muted colors with small dash lights. Consider fictionalizing the department's name and seal for the game.
slangAndCulture: General early-90s street fashion (mainstream, widely documented): oversized white T-shirts, often sold in multi-packs; heavy work pants such as Dickies-style 874s ($15-20) and creased khakis worn baggy; flannel/Pendleton-style shirts buttoned only at the top (a West Coast look); team 'Starter'-style satin or puffy jackets and half-zip pullovers ($100-150, prized and sometimes stolen); pro-team snapbacks and jerseys, with Raiders gear made iconic by West Coast rap; baggy jeans and overalls with one strap down; Cross Colours / Karl Kani-style colorful streetwear; bucket hats.

Footwear: canvas high-top Chuck-style sneakers (~$30), white leather low-tops and classic 'Cortez'-style runners, and $100+ basketball shoes (a new Jordan model came out in 1993). Suede shoes and Timberland-style boots are more East Coast. Minor detail: in the early 90s, media widely repeated rumors that certain shoe brands' initials were read as color-coded insults.

Accessories: bandanas ('rags', 'flags') worn as headbands or tied on the head, draped from a back pocket, or wrapped around a wrist; wrap-around 'Locs'-style dark sunglasses; gold rope chains, gold teeth/fronts, a pager on the waistband; hairstyles such as fades, braids, cornrows, a fading high-top fade, and slicked hair.

Crip markers as shown in mainstream media (films like 'Colors' 1988, 'Boyz n the Hood' 1991, 'Menace II Society' 1993, and news coverage): the color blue (blue bandanas, blue laces, blue team gear such as navy, royal blue or light blue); greeting and address 'cuz' / 'cuh' and 'what's crackin''; the 'C-walk' (Crip walk) dance; media commonly report Crips avoiding or crossing out the letter B and avoiding the word 'blood'; a bandana on the left side is often depicted.

Blood markers as shown in mainstream media: the color red (red bandanas, red laces, red team gear); greeting and address 'blood' / 'bool' and 'what's poppin''; media commonly report Bloods swapping C for B (e.g., 'bool' for 'cool') and avoiding the word 'cuz'; a bandana on the right side is often depicted; the five-pointed star is commonly cited as a Blood symbol and the six-pointed star as a Crip symbol.

Both sides, as depicted: 'set' or 'hood' means the local subgroup, usually named after a street, park or neighborhood; 'O.G.' = original gangster / veteran; 'Y.G.' / 'baby' = younger member; 'homie', 'loc', 'dog', 'fool' as address; 'representin'', 'claim', 'mob', 'throwing up' signs, 'jumped in' (initiation, a common media trope), 'flamed up' / 'dipped in blue' (head-to-toe in one color), 'mark' / 'buster' = a coward or outsider. Wall graffiti 'roll calls' listing nicknames is a common film visual.

General early-90s slang: 'word', 'word up', 'phat', 'fresh', 'fly', 'dope', 'da bomb', 'all that', 'booyah', 'bounce' (leave), 'kickin' it', 'chill', 'my bad', 'talk to the hand', 'boo-yah', 'straight up', 'fo' shizzle' (popularized around 1993 by Snoop and Dre), 'G-thang', 'it's all good', 'mad' (very, East Coast), 'sprung', 'hella' (Northern California), 'played out', 'trippin'', 'wack'.

Midwest flavor: in Omaha these styles would mix with local Midwest culture: Husker red is everywhere, so red clothing alone did not mark anyone. Winter Starter jackets, Chicago Bulls gear (red, black), Kansas City Royals (blue), and seed/farm caps are also common. A realistic touch is NPCs in red Husker sweatshirts who are simply football fans.

Design note for the fictional sets: to avoid accidentally matching real Omaha groups, give fictional sets invented street/park names or clearly made-up neighborhood names instead of real Omaha street names, and never use real people's names or nicknames.
northOmahaHistory: North Omaha, especially the Near North Side along North 24th Street, has long been the heart of Omaha's African American community (verified). By the 1940s the corner of 24th & Lake was a bustling hub of Black-owned businesses, stores, professional offices, theaters, a bowling alley, pool halls and even a miniature golf course. The Jewell Building's Dreamland Ballroom made the strip a stop on the national jazz circuit; famous big-band stars played there (general knowledge, high). The Omaha Star, founded July 9, 1938 by publisher Mildred Brown, is Nebraska's oldest Black weekly newspaper, with its office at 2216 N. 24th Street. The Fair Deal Cafe at 2118 N. 24th Street was opened in 1954 by Charlie and Audentria 'Denny' Hall and ran until 2003, so it was still open in 1993. It was known as Omaha's 'Black City Hall' for the business, political and social organizing that happened over its tables. The Great Plains Black History Museum was founded in 1975 to preserve the region's African American history; the founder being Bertha Calloway and its 1993 location being the old Webster Telephone Exchange building near 22nd & Lake are general knowledge, medium confidence. Malcolm X was born in Omaha in 1925 (general knowledge, high). The community also carries hard history. Starting with a July 4, 1966 uprising at 24th & Lake after a 103-degree day, a series of civil disturbances in the late 1960s damaged the 24th Street business corridor, against a backdrop of long-standing discriminatory policing. Decades of disinvestment followed. In the 1970s and 80s the city and state cut the North Freeway (U.S. 75) through the neighborhood. Local historians estimate about 2,000 homes, businesses and churches were destroyed, physically dividing the community. The stretch north of Lake Street to Sorensen Parkway opened November 15, 1988, so in 1993 the freeway was a new concrete scar through older blocks. Public housing was a big part of the landscape. The Logan Fontenelle Homes, a 1938-39 New Deal project running from 20th to 24th Streets north of Paul Street, once housed more than 2,100 people in 550+ units. After residents won a 1991 civil-rights lawsuit against the Omaha Housing Authority and HUD, it was being demolished in the early 1990s and was replaced by the lower-density, mixed-income Conestoga neighborhood by the mid-90s. Other projects in the area included Hilltop, Pleasantview and Spencer Homes. In 1993 North 24th Street is a mix of surviving family businesses, historic churches, the Omaha Star office, barbershops and beauty salons, soul-food and rib spots, corner stores, vacant lots and boarded storefronts, all alongside strong churches, block clubs, citizen patrols and community organizers working to keep the neighborhood together. For respectful flavor text, show North Omaha as a proud, resilient community with deep jazz, press, church and civil-rights roots, not only as a backdrop for crime. Consider fictionalizing specific living businesses.
pricesIn1993: Federal minimum wage: $4.25/hour (in effect since April 1991; general knowledge, high).
Gasoline, regular unleaded: about $1.05-1.15/gallon; U.S. average about $1.11 (general knowledge, approximate). Pump signs like '1.09 9/10'.
First-class postage stamp: 29 cents (1991-1995; general knowledge, high).
Local payphone call: 25 cents in most places, a few still 20 cents (approximate).
Can of soda from a vending machine: 50-60 cents; 2-liter bottle about $1.09-1.29 (approximate).

Fast food: burger-joint 'big' signature burger about $2.00-2.30 (The Economist's 1993 U.S. Big Mac price was about $2.28; medium); plain hamburger about 59-69 cents; value meal about $2.99-3.49 (approximate). Nebraska touches: Runza sandwiches, Godfather's Pizza (founded in Omaha); consider parody names.
Movie ticket: about $4.00-4.50 (U.S. average about $4.14; medium); matinee about $2.50-3.
Gallon of milk about $2.40-2.80; loaf of bread about 75 cents-$1.25; dozen eggs about 85-90 cents (approximate).
Pack of cigarettes: about $1.80-2.10 (1993 saw a major brand price cut, 'Marlboro Friday', April 2, 1993; medium).
Newspaper: about 35-50 cents daily (approximate; Omaha World-Herald's exact 1993 price unverified). Nebraska Lottery scratch ticket: $1 (from about Sept 1993; medium).
Cassette album about $8-10; CD about $12-16; VHS rental $2-3; arcade game 25-50 cents (approximate).
Clothing: Starter-style team jacket $100-150; name-brand basketball shoes $80-125+; Dickies-style work pants $15-20; canvas high-tops about $30; white tee 3-pack about $8-10 (approximate).

Housing and cars: 1-2 bedroom apartment in Omaha roughly $300-500/month; average new car about $16,000-17,000; a beat-up used boxy sedan a few hundred to $1,500 (approximate). U.S. median household income about $31,000 (general knowledge, medium).
radioAndMusic: Authentic naming rule: U.S. radio stations west of the Mississippi use call signs starting with 'K', so every fictional Omaha station should be K___ (e.g., fictional 'KBNC 94.1 The Bounce', 'K-HOT 101.7 Hip-Hop & R&B', 'KNOR 89.3 North O Community Radio', 'KORN Country 98.5', 'KRVR 104.5 The River - Rock', 'KFLD AM 1290 News-Talk-Husker Sports', 'KSOL La Tejana 1020 AM'). Check that fictional call letters don't match real stations.

West Coast G-funk and gangsta rap dominate 1993: Dr. Dre's 'The Chronic' (released Dec 1992, huge all through 1993, 'Nuthin' but a G Thang'), Ice Cube ('It Was a Good Day'), Snoop Doggy Dogg's 'Doggystyle' (Nov 1993), 2Pac ('I Get Around', 'Keep Ya Head Up'), Cypress Hill, MC Eiht / 'Menace II Society' soundtrack (general knowledge, high). For the game, use sound-alike or original tracks, since licensing real songs is expensive.

East Coast hip-hop: Wu-Tang Clan's debut (Nov 1993), A Tribe Called Quest's 'Midnight Marauders' (Nov 1993), Naughty by Nature ('Hip Hop Hooray'), Onyx ('Slam'), House of Pain ('Jump Around', 1992), Queen Latifah ('U.N.I.T.Y.', late 1993) (general knowledge).
Party / bass rap: Tag Team 'Whoomp! (There It Is)' and 95 South 'Whoot, There It Is' (1993), Duice 'Dazzey Duks', Miami bass (general knowledge).

R&B / new jack swing / quiet storm: SWV ('Weak'), Janet Jackson ('That's the Way Love Goes'), Jodeci, Boyz II Men, Mary J. Blige, Toni Braxton, Silk, H-Town, Salt-N-Pepa ('Shoop', fall 1993). A late-night 'quiet storm' slow-jam show with dedications fits well (general knowledge).
Top 40 pop of 1993: UB40 'Can't Help Falling in Love', Whitney Houston 'I Will Always Love You', Ace of Base 'All That She Wants', 4 Non Blondes 'What's Up' (general knowledge).
Rock / alternative / grunge: Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Stone Temple Pilots, Smashing Pumpkins; plus classic rock stations (general knowledge).
Country is dominant on Nebraska radio: Garth Brooks, Brooks & Dunn, Reba, line-dance hits (general knowledge).

Gospel on Sunday mornings (fits North Omaha's church culture), jazz and blues heritage shows honoring 24th Street's Dreamland past, and Tejano / regional Mexican music reflecting South Omaha's growing Latino community tied to the meatpacking plants (general knowledge, medium).

AM talk and sports: Husker football play-by-play on fall Saturdays, Royals baseball, CWS updates in June, farm reports with grain and cattle prices, and repeated flood-stage and severe-weather bulletins in July 1993.

Ambient ad ideas: car dealership jingles, 'live racing at Ak-Sar-Ben', 'see the world's largest indoor jungle at the zoo', pager/beeper store ads ('No credit? No problem!'), furniture rent-to-own, 1-900 hotlines, sandbag volunteer PSAs, and military recruiting spots (Offutt).
sportsFacts: 1993 College World Series (June 4-12, Rosenblatt Stadium): LSU champion, 8-0 over Wichita State in the final before 20,286; coach Skip Bertman; pitcher Brett Laxton; MOP Todd Walker; LSU's second title (verified).

Omaha Royals: Triple-A affiliate of the Kansas City Royals in the American Association (1969-1997), home at Rosenblatt Stadium; Warren Buffett threw out the first pitch of the April 16, 1993 home opener (verified).
Omaha Racers: 1992-93 CBA champions; coach Mike Thibault; celebration rally at Westroads Mall May 4, 1993; played at Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum (verified).
Omaha Lancers: USHL junior hockey team founded 1986; home ice at Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum in this era (verified that they moved to Civic Auditorium only in 2009).

Nebraska Cornhuskers 1993: 11-0 regular season, 7-0 Big Eight, ranked #2, then lost the Jan 1, 1994 Orange Bowl 18-16 to #1 Florida State on a missed last-second field goal (verified). Coach Tom Osborne and QB Tommie Frazier (general knowledge, high). The previous Jan 1, 1993 Orange Bowl was also a loss to Florida State, played in the rain (verified).

Ak-Sar-Ben horse racing: declining crowds (1992 average about 3,500/day, lowest in 59 years) as Missouri casinos opened in 1993; a seven-furlong chute was added in 1993 (verified). Closed Aug 7, 1995.
Kansas City Royals: 1993 was George Brett's final season; Royals Stadium renamed Kauffman Stadium on July 2, 1993 (general knowledge, medium-high).

National: Chicago Bulls won their third straight NBA title (June 20, 1993); Michael Jordan retired Oct 6, 1993; Toronto Blue Jays won the World Series (Oct 23, 1993); Florida State's Charlie Ward won the 1993 Heisman (general knowledge, high).
